what_its_for: Eravacycline is an antibiotic used to treat serious belly (abdominal) infections caused by bacteria. It is given to adults who have complicated infections inside the abdomen, such as infections after surgery or infections involving the stomach and intestines.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein at a hospital or clinic. A healthcare professional will prepare and give you each dose. You will NOT take this medicine as a pill at home. Each infusion takes about 60 minutes.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 1 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given every 12 hours (twice a day) for 4 to 14 days. Your doctor will decide how many days you need treatment based on your infection. Your dose may be adjusted if you are taking certain other medicines, so always tell your doctor about everything you take.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a hospital or clinic setting, a missed dose is unlikely. If you miss a scheduled infusion appointment, contact your doctor or nurse right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up doses.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. The hospital or clinic pharmacy handles all storage. In general, the prepared IV solution must be used within a specific time frame and kept refrigerated or at room temperature as directed by pharmacy staff.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are taking blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin), as eravacycline may make them work stronger and increase your bleeding risk. Avoid becoming pregnant while receiving this medicine, as tetracycline-type antibiotics like this one can harm an unborn baby and affect bone and tooth development. Avoid breastfeeding during treatment. Tell your doctor about all vitamins, supplements, and medications you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or nurse right away if you experience: severe diarrhea or diarrhea that is watery or bloody (this could be a serious gut infection called C. diff), signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, nausea or vomiting that is severe, unusual bruising or bleeding, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Also tell your team if you feel your IV site is painful, swollen, or red.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting treatment, but it is very important to complete the full course of treatment your doctor prescribed even if you feel better. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can harm your unborn baby, especially affecting bone and tooth development. Tell your doctor immediately if you are or become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Avoid breastfeeding during treatment and discuss with your doctor. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in patients under 18 years old. Older adults and patients with kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will monitor you closely, though dose adjustments are generally not needed for most patients with kidney problems. Patients with severe liver disease may need a dose adjustment.
